hops.afterHeading: The cochlea as a frequency map, and its amplifier
hops.title: Healthy ears give off sound
hops.text: Most of us picture the ear as a one-way microphone. In 1978 David Kemp put a tiny microphone in human ear canals, played soft clicks, and recorded echoes coming back out more than five milliseconds later. He found them in all the healthy ears he tested and in none with cochlear deafness: energy leaking back out of the cochlea's active amplifier. Some ears go further and hum with no sound going in at all; sensitive scans found these faint tones in 83% of women and 62% of men tested. Hospitals now screen newborns' hearing quickly by playing gentle clicks into the ear and listening for the cochlea's echo.

sources.citation: Kemp DT. Stimulated acoustic emissions from within the human auditory system. J Acoust Soc Am. 1978;64(5):1386-1391.
Penner MJ, Zhang T. Prevalence of spontaneous otoacoustic emissions in adults revisited. Hear Res. 1997;103(1-2):28-34.
Kemp DT, Ryan S. Otoacoustic emission tests in neonatal screening programmes. Acta Otolaryngol Suppl. 1991;482:73-84.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A sleeping newborn with a small soft probe at its ear and faint ripples drifting outward from the ear.
image.caption: A healthy cochlea's amplifier adds so much energy that some of it leaks back out as sound.

hops.title: A fly that hears direction across half a millimetre
hops.text: Ormia ochracea is a night-active fly that finds its hosts, calling crickets, by ear. It locates a sound source to within two degrees, as precisely as you, yet its eardrums sit less than half a millimetre apart. By this section's ITD formula, the arrival-time difference across that gap is at most a microsecond or two, and near straight ahead a two-degree change shifts it by only about 50 nanoseconds. Its answer is mechanical: a tiny bridge of cuticle joins the two eardrums, so each one's motion tugs on the other and their difference grows before the nerves see it. Engineers have since modelled directional hearing-aid microphones on its ears.

sources.citation: Miles RN, Robert D, Hoy RR. Mechanically coupled ears for directional hearing in the parasitoid fly Ormia ochracea. J Acoust Soc Am. 1995;98(6):3059-3070.
Mason AC, Oshinsky ML, Hoy RR. Hyperacute directional hearing in a microscale auditory system. Nature. 2001;410(6829):686-690.
Lakes-Harlan R, Lehmann GU. Parasitoid flies exploiting acoustic communication of insects: comparative aspects of independent functional adaptations. J Comp Physiol A. 2015;201(1):123-132.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small golden-brown fly on a blade of grass at night, facing a singing field cricket on a nearby stem.
image.caption: Eardrums half a millimetre apart, joined by a cuticle bridge, let this fly locate sound as precisely as you.

hops.title: Ear-rinse water and a Nobel Prize
hops.text: At a Vienna ear clinic, Robert Bárány kept seeing patients turn dizzy while their ears were rinsed. One said he only got dizzy when the water was too cool, so Bárány asked the nurse for warmer water. She brought very hot water, and the patient was dizzy again, but now his eyes jerked the opposite way. Body-temperature water did nothing. Bárány pictured a bath-water tank, with cooled fluid sinking. Later models stress that the cupula seals the canal, so the temperature difference mainly pushes on it as pressure. Either way it bends with the head still. News of his 1914 Nobel Prize reached him in a Russian prisoner-of-war camp.
